sourceNote: Juan de Plasencia's Tagalog worship account is included among his 1589 relations. It calls a ritual specialist catolonan and says a woman or a man could hold that role. It is a Spanish missionary's colonial account, not a neutral description of every community or direct proof of conditions before Spanish contact. The child-facing text paraphrases only the narrow role fact and does not reproduce disparaging or graphic source language.

fields.title: Who Could Guide a Ceremony?
fields.content:
Bayani takes you to an imagined community gathering. People listen while a ritual specialist called a babaylan helps guide a ceremony. This scene was made for the lesson; it is not a record of one real gathering. Some communities used the word babaylan, while other communities had different words and practices.

Now study a dated written source. In 1589, a Spanish missionary named Juan de Plasencia wrote about Tagalog customs. He used the Tagalog word catolonan for a ritual specialist and reported that a woman or a man could hold that role. This gives us one historical example of women taking part in community religious leadership.

Plasencia wrote after Spaniards had arrived. His descriptions include his own religious judgments, so we use only what the source reports about a role. One Tagalog account cannot tell us how every Philippine community lived, or exactly what happened before Spanish contact. The imagined gathering is not a record of the Tagalog people described by Plasencia.

Explore the clues. Who is named in the source, what role could a woman hold, and what is still unknown? You do not need to take part in a ceremony to learn about it.

fields.keyTermDefinition: A babaylan was a ritual specialist in some early Philippine communities, including parts of the Visayas. A 1589 Tagalog account used a different word, catolonan, for a ritual role that a woman or a man could hold. Names and practices varied.
fields.historicalInsight: A 1589 Tagalog account by Spanish missionary Juan de Plasencia reports that a catolonan could be a woman or a man. His account reflects a colonial writer's viewpoint and cannot describe every community or settle exactly what happened before Spanish contact.

fields.content:
Now connect a named object with the questions in this mission. The Manunggul Jar comes from Palawan and is associated with burial practices. Its lid has two figures in a boat. A Cultural Center of the Philippines interpretation connects this imagery with a journey after death.

Separate three statements. Observation: the lid has boat-and-figure imagery. Interpretation: the imagery has been understood in connection with beliefs about death. Limit: one object does not show every belief in the islands, and it does not scientifically prove an afterlife. This illustration is a source-summary card, not a photograph of the original jar.

Compare a written source too. In 1589, Juan de Plasencia reported that a Tagalog ritual specialist called a catolonan could be a woman or a man. The account was written after Spanish arrival and includes the writer's own religious judgments. It is evidence of a reported role in that setting, not a description of every woman or every community. Keep the imagined gathering separate from the Tagalog setting described in the account.

Across the mission, beliefs could shape how people treated places, rituals could express thanks or hopes, and oral traditions could pass on knowledge. The jar, the written account and Hudhud are different kinds of evidence from different settings. Save useful clues in your journal. Next, explore Islam and cultural exchange without treating all communities as identical.

learningHelp.explanation: Name the source and its setting before making a claim. A jar's design, a written account and a living chant can each teach something different; none describes every community.

fields.learningObjective: Explain community beliefs, ritual leadership and oral traditions with named sources, then describe what each source can and cannot show.
learningObjectives: Explain how ritual specialists could guide ceremonies in some communities.
Use a 1589 Tagalog account to identify one ritual role a woman or a man could hold, without applying it to every community.
Distinguish an invented classroom tale from a documented oral tradition.
Compare traditional performance and additional teaching supports without assuming complete sameness over time.
Use the Manunggul Jar as a named artifact for interpreting a belief with limits.
Respect different traditions without requiring personal religious practice or disclosure.
fields.lessonRecap: Some communities had ritual specialists, but names and practices varied. A 1589 Tagalog account by Juan de Plasencia says a catolonan could be a woman or a man; his colonial viewpoint and later writing date limit what we can conclude about all earlier communities. Our babaylan gathering and bird tale are fictional. Hudhud is a documented Ifugao tradition, while the Manunggul Jar is a named artifact for interpreting particular beliefs. None proves that every community followed the same practice or that a supernatural claim is scientifically true. Traditions can continue while some ways of teaching or recording them change.

fields.question: What did Plasencia's 1589 account about Tagalog customs report about a catolonan?
fields.optionA: Only the datu could guide a ceremony
fields.optionB: A woman or a man could serve as a ritual specialist
fields.optionC: Every community used the same title for this role
fields.optionD: The account listed every woman's daily work
fields.explanation: The 1589 Tagalog account says a catolonan could be a woman or a man. It reports one named ritual role; it does not describe every community.
fields.historicalClue: Look for who could hold the Tagalog role named in the 1589 account. Keep the writer's setting and limits in mind.
fields.learningPoint: A dated Tagalog account reports women as possible ritual specialists, while one source cannot describe every community.

answerExplanations.A: The account names a catolonan as a ritual specialist; it does not say only the datu could guide a ceremony.
answerExplanations.B: Plasencia reported that a woman or a man could be a catolonan in the Tagalog setting he described.
answerExplanations.C: The account uses a Tagalog term. Other communities could use different terms and practices.
answerExplanations.D: The account describes one ritual role, not every kind of work done by every woman.

fields.question: A museum label describes a woman guiding a ceremony in the Tagalog setting reported by Plasencia in 1589. Which label fits that account?
fields.optionA: Datu: the only person permitted to guide a ceremony
fields.optionB: Catolonan: a ritual specialist whose role could be held by a woman or a man
fields.optionC: Babaylan: the exact word used in this Tagalog account
fields.optionD: Bayani: a person named in the historical account
fields.explanation: The account uses catolonan for the Tagalog ritual role and says a woman or a man could hold it. A museum label should match that source and setting.
fields.historicalClue: Match the role and term to the 1589 Tagalog account, rather than to the imagined scene.
fields.learningPoint: Women could hold a named ritual role in the reported Tagalog setting; keep regional terms and source limits clear.

answerExplanations.A: The account names a catolonan as a ritual specialist; it does not restrict this role to a datu.
answerExplanations.B: This label keeps the term, ritual role and inclusion of women reported in the Tagalog account.
answerExplanations.C: Babaylan appears in our imagined scene. The translated Tagalog account uses catolonan.
answerExplanations.D: Bayani is our learning guide, not a person named in the historical account.

fields.question: In Plasencia's 1589 Tagalog account, who could be a catolonan?
fields.optionA: A woman or a man serving as a ritual specialist
fields.optionB: Only a datu and no one else
fields.explanation: The account says a woman or a man could hold the catolonan ritual role in the Tagalog setting it describes.
fields.learningPoint: A woman could hold the named ritual role in this dated Tagalog account; the example does not describe every community.
fields.hint: Look back at the named role in the Tagalog source card. Who did the writer say could hold it?

answerHints.B: A datu was a leader, but the source names another community role. Who could hold it?
answerHints.C: Does the 1589 account rule out women, or does it name them too?
answerHints.D: The source talks about a particular ritual role, not a task given to all children.

answerExplanations.A: The account says a woman or a man could be a catolonan.
answerExplanations.B: The account does not limit the catolonan role to a datu.
answerExplanations.C: The account includes women as well as men in this named role.
answerExplanations.D: The source does not say that every child held this role.

fields.question: Our made-up scene shows a babaylan guiding a ceremony. A 1589 Tagalog account says a catolonan could be a woman or a man. Which conclusion fits both clues?
fields.optionA: Some communities had ritual specialists, and the dated Tagalog account records women as possible leaders in its setting
fields.optionB: The imagined babaylan is the same person named in the Tagalog account
fields.optionC: Every early community used one title and one ceremony
fields.optionD: Only men could guide ceremonies in all communities
fields.explanation: The fictional babaylan scene shows a ritual specialist as a teaching example. The dated Tagalog account reports a role women or men could hold. Together they support a limited conclusion about ritual leadership, not one rule for every community.
fields.historicalClue: One clue is imagined; the other is a dated report about a Tagalog term. Look for what both show about ritual specialists without mixing the people or settings.
fields.learningPoint: Women could be ritual specialists in a named Tagalog account; different communities could use different titles and practices.
fields.hint: Ask what both clues show about ritual roles, then check which detail comes from the dated account.

answerHints.B: One scene is made up for the lesson. Can its character be named in the old account?
answerHints.C: The account describes a Tagalog role. Does that tell us every title and ceremony in the islands?
answerHints.D: Check who the 1589 account says could hold the catolonan role.

answerExplanations.A: Both clues show ritual leadership, and the dated Tagalog account includes women in its named role.
answerExplanations.B: A fictional babaylan cannot be the same person as someone in a historical source.
answerExplanations.C: One fictional scene and one Tagalog account cannot show identical practices everywhere.
answerExplanations.D: The 1589 account reports that a woman or a man could hold the ritual role.
